newsitem.title: USA: Russia's Rodionov begins U.S. talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Rodionov begins U.S. talks.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov on Tuesday began two days of talks with senior U.S. officials on boosting bilateral military cooperation despite Moscow's bitter opposition to NATO enlargement.

Rodionov was welcomed to the Pentagon by Defence Secretary William Cohen, where officials said they would discuss issues ranging from increased defence ties to nuclear arms cuts and security in Europe and the Pacific.

The defence chiefs were to hold a news conference before Rodionov met later on Tuesday with White House National Security Adviser Samuel Berger. He will meet on Wednesday with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright before departing for Hawaii and Japan.

The visit was Rodionov's first to Washington as defence minister and came as Russian President Boris Yeltsin stepped up his personal telephone diplomacy with NATO leaders but told Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to take a tough line in talks with the western alliance on its plans for enlargement.
Russia has given no official indication yet whether it will sign a document in Paris later this month establishing a new relationship with the western alliance after years of mistrust.

Meanwhile, Washington and Moscow have pledged to improve cooperation in areas such as military peacekeeping as the impoverished Russian military struggles to make the transition from life under Communist rule to a democratic society.
Cohen greeted Rodionov with a colourful Pentagon welcoming ceremony, including a 19-gun salute for the visitor, on the grassy Pentagon parade field.
Rodionov, a now-retired general who replaced Pavel Grachev as defence minister last year, stopped as he walked by the U.S. flag on the parade ground.
He faced the flag and its military bearer and bowed slightly before he and Cohen continued reviewing the military honour guard.

The Rodionov-Cohen meeting came a day after the Washington Times reported that some Russian strategic nuclear missiles had accidentally gone on alert status because of deteriorating technical equipment.

A senior Pentagon official said privately on Monday, however, that he saw no reason to fear an accidental or unauthorised launch because firing such weapons required special codes and high-level authorisation.
